extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics faculty, curriculum designers, and math educators interested in undergraduate core capstone design
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and running an undergraduate mathematics core-capstone course (junior/senior level) that uses Francis Su's Mathematics for Human Flourishing as a central text to connect mathematics to virtues, community, and students' ethical development. Includes course structure, readings, in-class activities, and assessment approaches emphasizing reflection over technical solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the four unifying capstone questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Core capstone courses should aim at answering a common set of questions: “What should matter to me?”, “How should we live together?”, “How can we understand the world?”, and “What will I do?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course was intended to accomplish a lot by organizing around these four questions; they provide the ends that capstones should achieve (synthesis of experience, ethical reflection, understanding) while allowing varied means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize college experience and emphasize change in thinking/ethical decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: A core capstone's goal is to synthesize the college experience, with an emphasis on how and why the student’s own thinking and ethical decision-making has changed during their time at college.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capstones should prompt students to reflect on development over time rather than simply demonstrating discrete skills; final products (essays) should tie personal growth to future actions (the 'What will I do?' question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to juniors/seniors and accessible across majors (no prerequisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Core capstone courses should be open to only junior or senior students and, ideally, require no prerequisites so students from any major can enroll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights a problem when capstones required 300-level prerequisites that made them inaccessible; course design should avoid unnecessary prerequisites to prevent a 'checkbox' bottleneck and increase enrollment accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a 'checkbox mentality' — design a fluid yet coherent core
rubrics_metrics.description: Curriculum should be designed to avoid 'checkbox mentality' by creating a fluid yet coherent core that allows variety of options without feeling like disjointed courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means (course design) should be determined to serve pedagogical ends (synthesis, reflection). The core should feel unified by shared questions rather than being a mere list of requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a principal text that frames mathematics as cultivating virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose central course texts (e.g., Francis Su’s Mathematics for Human Flourishing) that present mathematics as a practice that develops virtues (play, community, freedom, justice, charity) rather than solely as instrumental skill-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using MFHF as the main text allowed the instructor to address the capstone questions and foreground virtues; each chapter's focus on a virtue supplies thematic material for readings and reflection prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include interdisciplinary and complementary readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement the principal text with complementary books and readings (e.g., The Data Detective by Tim Harford, A Mathematician’s Lament by Paul Lockhart, passages from Aristotle and Poincaré) to broaden perspectives and connect mathematics to other domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary texts can provide different lenses (e.g., Harford uses virtues to view statistics) and help students see mathematics in varied humanistic and practical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign regular readings with nightly reflection questions (workload guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students completed readings for every class, roughly fifteen to twenty-five pages each night, and contemplated reflection questions for each of the readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, moderate reading loads plus directed reflection questions ensure students engage with the texts and prepare to discuss virtues and implications in class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a daily 'problem of the day' to reintroduce play and exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Each class period should feature a 'problem of the day' intended to help bring fun, play, and exploration back into doing math, especially for self‑proclaimed 'non-math' persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems are not primarily for assessing technical mastery but for fostering curiosity and lowering barriers—they serve as springboards for reflection about virtues developed when doing math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midterm reflections: analyze selected problems focusing on virtues, not solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Halfway through the course, students chose four previous problems of the day to analyze in a one-page reflection focused on the virtues the student cultivated when working through the problems rather than presenting solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment here is explicitly reflective: the purpose is to discuss cultivated virtues (e.g., patience, curiosity, community) and students are encouraged to describe their processes and personal growth rather than correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final essay: articulate cultivated virtues and future actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The final essay asks students to discuss the virtue or virtues they have cultivated most during their college careers and how this might affect their lives after college, tying to the core question 'What will I do?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final assessment should prompt actionable reflection and connect personal development in mathematics to future ethical or practical decisions; strong essays serve as prompts for the student's next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize authentic personal reflection in student work
rubrics_metrics.description: Student work should aim for authentic reflection rather than telling the instructor what they think the instructor wants to hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instructor valued papers where students genuinely reflected on how math cultivated community or other virtues (e.g., stories about working on problems with teammates or family). Authenticity is a quality marker for grading and course success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster community through collaborative problem-solving and stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Course design should encourage and value examples of community formation—students told stories of working on problems with sports teams, significant others, roommates, or family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments and in-class activities should create opportunities for collaborative engagement; evidence of community-building is treated as a positive outcome in reflections and assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure success by changes in student attitudes toward mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful course will lead students (including non-majors) to see mathematics differently—more hopeful, more appreciative, and more likely to incorporate math into their lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course evaluations and student comments (e.g., 'I feel like I appreciate math more than I used to') serve as outcome metrics indicating the course met its human-flourishing goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debunk the stereotype of mathematics as purely instrumental; present math as humane
rubrics_metrics.description: One aim of the course is to tear down the view of mathematics as only for the 'super elite' and instead build up mathematics as a humane endeavor done by humans for humans, with joys and struggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy, readings, and assessments should emphasize human elements of doing math (joy, frustration, hope) rather than purely technical proficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure course demand and sustainability (practical implementation constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make course offerings feasible and enrollable (e.g., no prerequisites, cross-listed/available to all majors) so that majors and non-majors can access the capstone without being blocked by scheduling or prerequisite gates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes initial scarcity of designated capstones and the benefit of designing a course that fills that institutional need (course was fully subscribed when offered).
